text: In Sri Lankan public law teaching, the Constitution is treated as the supreme law. Ordinary statutes and regulations must give way when they conflict with a constitutional provision. A student should therefore start any constitutional problem by naming the article that actually constrains the organ of state in the facts, not by quoting a later Act as if it could override the Constitution.

Fundamental rights petitions in this jurisdiction are typically discussed as a direct route to the Supreme Court under Article 126. The exam skill is to map the facts onto a named right (equality, freedom of speech, freedom from arbitrary arrest) and then ask whether an executive or administrative act infringed it, not whether a private neighbour was rude.

Natural justice is taught as two working maxims. Audi alteram partem means the person affected must be given a fair chance to be heard before an adverse decision. Nemo judex in causa sua means the decision-maker must not sit in their own cause. A disciplinary committee that both prosecutes and decides, without notice of the charge, fails both maxims.

Ultra vires is the idea that a public body may only do what its parent statute allows. If a licensing authority invents a fee or a ban that the Act never authorised, the decision is outside power even if the official thought it was sensible. Students should quote the empowering section and show the extra step that is not in it.

Contract formation still needs offer, acceptance, and consideration. Consideration is the price of the promise: something of value given in exchange. A bare promise to make a gift, with nothing moving the other way, is not a bargain the common-law courts will enforce as a contract, however moral the disappointment.

An invitation to treat is not an offer. A shop display, a catalogue price, and many advertisements invite customers to make offers. The shopkeeper may refuse to sell. Treating every displayed price as a binding offer is a common first-year mix-up and loses marks on problem questions.

Misrepresentation in contract is a false statement of fact that induces the other party to enter the contract. A statement of future intention is not automatically a misrepresentation unless it was never honestly held. Remedies split between rescission (unwinding) and damages depending on whether the statement was fraudulent, negligent, or innocent.

Exemption clauses are read strictly against the party who drafted them. If the clause is unusual or onerous, the drafter must show it was fairly brought to the other party's attention. A tiny footnote on the back of a ticket after the contract was already made will not usually do that work.

Negligence requires duty, breach, causation, and damage. Duty of care is not a feeling of moral responsibility; it is a legal relationship the courts recognise, classically neighbours who ought reasonably to have been in contemplation as affected by the act. A driver owes road users a duty; a passer-by who simply watches a stranger trip usually does not.

Causation in negligence is taught in two layers. Factual causation asks whether the harm would have occurred but for the breach. Legal causation then asks whether the harm is too remote, or whether a later event broke the chain. Both can fail even when the defendant was careless in the abstract.

Vicarious liability makes an employer answerable for a tort committed by an employee in the course of employment. The course-of-employment test looks at whether the wrongful act was a way of doing the job, even a forbidden way, rather than a frolic of the employee's own. Independent contractors are the usual contrast: the hirer is not vicariously liable for them on the same rule.

Occupiers' liability is about the duty owed to people who enter premises. Lawful visitors are owed a duty to take reasonable care that they are reasonably safe for the purpose of the visit. Trespassers are not owed the same package; the duty, if any, is narrower and fact-specific. A student who treats every injured person on land as a visitor will mis-state the standard.

Hearsay in evidence teaching is an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of what it asserts. The objection is that the speaker cannot be cross-examined in the box. Not every report of what someone said is hearsay: if the statement is offered only to show that words were spoken (notice, threat, reputation), it may be original evidence instead.

Burden and standard of proof split by forum. In a criminal trial the prosecution generally bears the burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt. In a civil claim the claimant generally proves their case on the balance of probabilities. Mixing the two standards in an answer is a fast way to lose a methods mark.

Theft is usually taught as dishonest appropriation of property belonging to another with intention to permanently deprive. Criminal misappropriation is a neighbouring idea used when property was originally received innocently (a found wallet, a mistaken overpayment) and later kept dishonestly. The exam contrast is how the property first came into the accused's hands.

Mens rea is the guilty mind that the definition of the offence requires: intention, knowledge, or sometimes recklessness. Actus reus is the prohibited conduct or result. An accident without the required mental element is not the same offence even if the physical result looks identical. Always name both elements before jumping to sentence.

Directors of a company owe fiduciary duties to the company: to act in good faith in its interests, to avoid secret profits, and not to place themselves in a position of conflict without informed consent. A director who diverts a corporate opportunity into a private side-company is the classic illustration used in company-law tutorials.

A company is a separate legal person from its shareholders. Limited liability means a member is not personally liable for the company's debts beyond what they agreed to contribute. Lifting the corporate veil is exceptional, not a general fairness tool. Partnership, by contrast, typically leaves partners jointly liable for firm debts.

The Prescription Ordinance is the local limitation statute students meet in civil procedure. Section 10 is the provision tutors use when drilling time-bars for certain classes of action: if the plaintiff slept on the claim beyond the prescribed period, the defendant may plead prescription even when the underlying right once existed. Always count from the date the cause of action accrued, not from the date the client first instructed counsel.

Land acquisition by the State is a public-law process with notice, inquiry, and compensation stages. A landowner who only complains that the project is politically inconvenient has not yet identified a legal defect. The better student looks for missing notice, a purpose outside the empowering law, or a compensation formula that ignores the statute.

A trust separates legal title (the trustee) from beneficial enjoyment (the beneficiary). The trustee must deal with the property for the beneficiary, not as if it were personal wealth. Mixing trust money with private money, or investing in a forbidden speculation, is a breach even if the trustee hoped to make a profit for everyone.

Specific performance is an equitable remedy that orders a party to carry out a contract rather than merely pay damages. It is discretionary and is classically refused for contracts of personal service and where damages would be adequate. Land contracts are the usual example where damages are treated as inadequate because each parcel is unique.

Judicial review is not an appeal on the merits. The court asks whether the public decision was lawful: jurisdiction, fairness of procedure, and whether relevant considerations were taken into account. Substituting the judge's preferred policy for the minister's is the error the course keeps warning against.

An affidavit is sworn written evidence. In interlocutory applications it is often the whole factual record. Hearsay in an affidavit is sometimes permitted at interim stage with the source identified, but a final trial still prefers oral evidence that can be tested. Students should not treat an untested affidavit paragraph as equivalent to a finding after cross-examination.
